stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED by ambulance one hour after ingesting an unknown number of amitriptyline 25 mg tablets from her partner's supply. She is drowsy but rousable to voice. Her pupils are dilated at 6 mm bilaterally with sluggish reaction, and her skin is warm and dry.

Her partner reports the bottle held approximately sixty tablets three days ago and is now empty. There is no history of coingestion or alcohol use. She has a background of adjustment disorder but no prior overdoses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 12; pupils 6 mm sluggish; warm dry skin; bowel sounds absent; urinary retention present
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia rate 128, QRS 128 milliseconds, terminal R in aVR of 4 mm; VBG pH 7.32, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus repeated to QRS narrowing
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms in TCA overdose is an indication for sodium bicarbonate bolus targeting pH 7.5 and QRS narrowing; reverses fast sodium channel blockade. (Source: eTG: Toxicology; ACEM Poison guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 0.5 to 2 mg over 3 minutes to reverse anticholinergic toxidrome
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it increases risk of seizures and asystole; sodium bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reverse suspected sedative co-ingestion
options.rationale: Flumazenil precipitates seizures particularly in mixed overdoses and pro-convulsant coingestants like TCA; not indicated here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus for arrhythmia prevention and rate control
options.rationale: Magnesium is used for torsades but does not treat sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate is the mechanism-directed antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous lidocaine loading 1 mg/kg followed by infusion at 1 to 4 mg/min
options.rationale: Lidocaine also blocks sodium channels and compounds TCA toxicity; contraindicated as first-line arrhythmia treatment in TCA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose combines anticholinergic toxidrome, sodium channel blockade (widening QRS, terminal R in aVR, hypotension) and alpha-1 blockade. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus is the mechanism-directed antidote for QRS above 100 ms or hypotension unresponsive to fluids, targeting pH 7.45 to 7.55. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines; refractory hypotension with noradrenaline. Physostigmine is contraindicated. Terminal R wave 3 mm or more in aVR predicts cardiotoxicity. Intralipid emulsion is a rescue option for cardiovascular collapse.
key_points: QRS 100 ms or more or terminal R in aVR 3 mm or more predicts TCA toxicity.
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus is first-line.
Target pH 7.45 to 7.55; narrow QRS as endpoint.
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose with QRS above 100 ms: 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV sodium bicarbonate boluses to pH 7.5 or QRS narrowing; physostigmine is a contraindication.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 3 years with excellent mood stability. She attends your general practice for her scheduled review. Her most recent 12-hour post-dose lithium level 6 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8). She reports no polyuria or polydipsia and no fine tremor. She takes no other psychotropic medications.

She is asymptomatic today. Weight is stable at 68 kg (BMI 24 kg/m2). She has no personal or family history of thyroid disease, no cardiac history, and no NSAID use. Her booking bloods on lithium initiation showed normal renal function, thyroid function, calcium, and ECG.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no tremor; no goitre palpable; euthymic mood
data_table.Investigations: Recent lithium level 0.7 mmol/L 6 months ago (target 0.6-0.8); no bloods today yet

lead_in: What is the appropriate monitoring schedule at this visit?

options.text: Substitute lithium level with 24-hour urinary lithium excretion every 3 months as the sole intervention
options.rationale: 24-hour urinary lithium is not routine practice; standard is 12-hour post-dose serum level. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Serum lithium level, urea and electrolytes, and thyroid function testing every 6 months in stable maintenance
options.rationale: RANZCP and eTG lithium monitoring in stable maintenance is lithium level, U and E, and TFTs every 6 months, with calcium annually and ECG when clinically indicated. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder; Australian eTG Psychotropic - Lithium)

options.text: Serum lithium level and renal function annually only in stable long-term maintenance
options.rationale: Annual monitoring is insufficient in maintenance; 6-monthly bloods including lithium level, U and E and TFTs are the standard. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Full monitoring panel weekly for 4 weeks then no further testing for 12 months if stable
options.rationale: Weekly bloods are for initiation and dose change; long-term maintenance uses 6-monthly monitoring. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Random lithium level and random calcium testing only in the presence of symptoms as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Routine 6-monthly scheduled monitoring detects subclinical thyroid or renal impairment before symptoms develop. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar disorder)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring per RANZCP and eTG in stable maintenance uses 6-monthly serum lithium (12 hours post-dose), U and E, and thyroid function tests, plus annual calcium level and clinically directed ECG. Baseline before initiation is renal function including eGFR, TFTs, calcium, ECG in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk, and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive age. Monitoring frequency increases with dose change, symptoms, or intercurrent illness (dehydration, NSAID use, ACE inhibitor initiation) that raises toxicity risk. Long-term lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism (up to 20 percent) and less commonly hyperparathyroidism. Target maintenance level in bipolar is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.
key_points: 6-monthly lithium level, U and E, TFTs in stable maintenance.
Annual calcium and clinically directed ECG.
Baseline renal, thyroid, calcium, ECG, and pregnancy test where relevant.
Long-term risks include NDI, CKD, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.
explanation.pearls: For a stable long-term lithium patient the 6-monthly schedule is 12-hour post-dose lithium level, U and E and TFTs, with calcium annually; watch for hypothyroidism which affects up to 20 percent.
